title: CAPTURE RSV: Comprehensive Assessment of Pediatric RSV Infections requiring hospitalization in the Updated RSV Immunization Era – A German Multicenter Retrospective Cohort Study
summary:
What is the study about?
The CAPTURE-RSV study investigates how severely infants under one year of age in Germany are affected by RSV infections when hospitalization is required. RSV stands for "Respiratory Syncytial Virus" – a common virus that can cause serious respiratory illness in babies.

Why is this important?
New strategies to protect children from RSV – so-called immunization strategies – have recently become available. We want to find out how effective these strategies are and which children are at particular risk of developing severe disease.

What exactly is being studied?
The study collects data from hospitals across Germany. Medical records of infants under one year who are hospitalized due to RSV during the autumn and winter of 2024/2025 will be analyzed. Among other things, we will look at:
- How severely the children were affected – for example, how long they stayed in hospital, whether they needed intensive care, or whether complications occurred.
- How reliable hospital coding based on ICD-10 diagnoses is, by comparing it to actual RSV test results.
- Which children are at higher risk – based on age, pre-existing conditions, or immunization status.
- What treatments and diagnostic measures were used and how the illness progressed.
- How the situation in the 2024/2025 season compares to previous years.

How is the study conducted?
This is a retrospective study, meaning only data already collected during routine medical care will be used – with no additional effort or procedures required for the children or their families. All data will be fully anonymized and securely transferred using a central REDCap system.

Who is participating in the study?
A total of at least 490 anonymized patient records from approximately 15 hospitals across Germany will be analyzed. All infants under one year of age who were hospitalized due to RSV during the 2024/2025 RSV season are eligible for inclusion.

Why is the study important?
With the results of the CAPTURE-RSV study, we aim to better understand:
- How RSV infections progress today, now that new protective measures are available.
- Which children need particular protection.
- How we can further improve hospital care and prevention.

Key questions the study addresses:
- How severely do infants get ill from RSV – even with new protective measures?
- Which children are most at risk for severe illness?
- How accurate are current diagnosis codes (ICD-10) in identifying RSV cases?
- Have the numbers of severe RSV cases changed since new immunizations were introduced?
- What can we learn from treatments and outcomes to improve prevention in the future?

interventions.name: Infants (<1 year) of any gender with acute RSV infection requiring hospitalization in Germany

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
• Study population: Infants of any gender <12 months of age at hospitalization with positive PCR or rapid test evidence for RSV during RSV season 2024/2025 as defined by the RKI
o Risk factors sub-cohort: At least one of the following risk factors for severe disease in RSV infection are present
- Chronic lung disease (e.g., bronchopulmonary dysplasia, interstitial lung disease, cystic fibrosis, congenital respiratory abnormalities)
- Severe cardiac disorders and/or complex congenital heart defects (e.g., aortic arch abnormalities, hypoplastic left heart syndrome, pulmonary atresia, tricuspid atresia, Fallot tetralogy, large artery transposition, partial or total pulmonary vein defect, other heart valve abnormalities) 
- Neuromuscular disease (e.g., autonomic dysfunction or dysautonomia, autonomic nervous system instability, corpus callosum agenesis or hypoplasia, muscular dystrophy)
- Severe congenital or acquired immunodeficiency
- Syndromal disease (e.g., trisomy 21)
- Smokers in the family
• Vaccinated sub-cohort: Evidence of at least one timely active or passive vaccination against RSV prior to disease onset (e.g., palivizumab, nirsevimab, maternal immunization with RSV preF)
Unvaccinated sub-cohort: No active or passive vaccination against RSV prior to disease onset
Exclusion criteria:
• Patient records where RSV infection was only documented as a secondary diagnosis or incidental finding and is not considered a primary or substantial reason for hospitalization
• Patient records with hospitalization outside the defined RSV season 2024/2025 as defined by RKI
• Patient records with missing or incomplete clinical data that make clear assessment of inclusion criteria or vaccination status impossible
